records.place: Cutchogue, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Musée
wine.grapes: Bordeaux grapes in a blend that changes yearly: Merlot led the early vintages, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot; later ones give Petit Verdot and Malbec more.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards at Cutchogue on the North Fork, on sandy glacial soils that drain fast, between Long Island Sound and the Peconic Bay.
wine.making: Made from the house's grapes of the North Fork. By the house's own account every wine of the cellar is fermented with the wild yeasts of the place rather than bought cultures. The wine is then aged in barrel before bottling, and its blend is settled anew each year.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and cassis with cedar, tobacco leaf and a cool, saline edge from the sea; medium to full in body, with moderate alcohol, crisp acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it gains savoury depth over its first decade and a strong vintage keeps well beyond it.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: French for museum: the house's leading red blend, under a label made from an artist's work.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Musée is Bedell Cellars' grand red from Cutchogue on the North Fork: a blend of the Bordeaux grapes whose first label carried a daguerreotype of the estate's grapes by Chuck Close. It is cool, saline and firm, so decant it.
records.story: Bedell Cellars began in 1980, when its founder planted his first vines on a farm at Cutchogue, seven years after the first vinifera went into a potato field in the same village. Through the 1980s and 1990s the house built its name on Merlot, the grape that leads on the North Fork, and in 1986 the North Fork of Long Island won its own American Viticultural Area. In 1999 the estate was sold to Michael Lynne (1941 to 2019), the film executive of New Line Cinema, who kept the founder on as winemaker and set out to raise the house to the serious end of the fork. He brought in contemporary artists to make the labels, and the painter and photographer Chuck Close (1940 to 2021) made a daguerreotype of the very grapes picked for the first Musée, the 2005. In 2013 the house's Merlot of 2009 was poured at the luncheon of the presidential inauguration in Washington, by the house's account the first New York wine served at an inauguration. The house holds that it ferments every wine with wild yeasts alone. For a sommelier, Musée is the North Fork's answer to the question of whether Long Island makes a red to keep.

others.name: Merlot
others.note: The house's grape of record; the 2009 was poured at the inaugural luncheon of 2013.

others.name: Taste Red
others.note: A second red blend of the house, for drinking sooner than Musée.

traps: Musée is a blend whose grapes change with the vintage, not a varietal Merlot, though Merlot is the grape the house is known for.
The wine poured at the 2013 inauguration was the 2009 Merlot, not Musée.
Bedell is at Cutchogue on the North Fork, not in the Hamptons on the South Fork.

cards.front: Bedell Musée: what is on its label, and who made it?

report: Founded 1980 and the sale of 1999 rest on the house's Heritage page; one press account gives 2000 for the sale, so the house's year is taught.

Musée's debut vintage 2005 rests on Edible Manhattan and a retailer's note; its grapes vary: about four fifths Merlot in the early vintages by the New York Cork Report of 2008, Petit Verdot and Malbec leading in 2019 by the house's store page, so no share is taught.

The barrel regimen (fifteen months in French oak, half new, by one 2008 account only) is left out for want of a second source, and so is the claim, in one retailer's note only, that Musée is made only in strong vintages.
Wild yeast fermentation is the house's own claim on its winemaking page and is hedged as such.
The inauguration fact is the 2009 Merlot, not Musée, by the Senate's luncheon programme and Wine Spectator; the first New York wine claim is the house's and is hedged.
The founder is living and is not named; the label artists other than Chuck Close are living and are not named; Taste Red's place in the range rests on the house's store only.
The glass note is drawn from the house's own account of its style (moderate alcohol, crisp, saline) and the varietal make up; no independent tasting note was read.

records.place: Peconic, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Old Vines Merlot
wine.grapes: Merlot, from the house's oldest vines.
wine.sites: The oldest blocks of the house's estate vineyard at Peconic on the North Fork, planted in its first decades on sandy, fast draining glacial soils.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the house judges able to give a wine of depth and long life, from its oldest Merlot vines. The wine is aged in barrel and then held back in the cellar for years, so it reaches the market long after the vintage, and the house keeps a library of older bottles and magnums.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and dried fig with cedar, tobacco and leather as it ages; medium to full in body, with fresh acidity, firm but fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released with age already on it, it keeps improving in a cool cellar; by the house's own tastings of its library its Old Vines reds peak at fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand an older bottle upright and decant it gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's tier from its oldest vineyard blocks, made only in strong vintages.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Lenz Winery's Old Vines Merlot comes from the oldest vines of one of the North Fork's early estates, planted at Peconic from 1978. It is held back for years before release, so it arrives savoury and ready; decant an older bottle off its sediment.
records.story: The Lenz Winery began in 1978, when the Lenz family planted vines on a farm at Peconic on the North Fork, five years after the first vinifera of Long Island went into the ground at Cutchogue nearby. Theirs was one of the island's early estates. In 1988, ten years on, the winery passed to new owners, who kept the founders' name on the label and set the house on its course of patient, long lived wines. From the early 1990s the house held back part of its strongest red vintages, which became the library from which it sells older bottles and magnums. It also took to comparative blind tastings, setting its wines beside well known wines of Europe and California to test the North Fork's claim. The Old Vines tier sits at the top of the range, drawn from the oldest blocks and made only in years the house judges able to give depth and long life. For a sommelier, the Old Vines Merlot shows what time does to a North Fork Merlot, which few houses on the island let a guest taste.

others.name: Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The red of the same Old Vines tier, from the house's old Cabernet Sauvignon vines.

others.name: Estate Selection Merlot
others.note: The house's Merlot below the Old Vines tier, for drinking sooner.

traps: Lenz releases its Old Vines Merlot years after the vintage, so an old date on a new bottle is the house style, not old stock.
Lenz is at Peconic on the North Fork, not on the South Fork among the Hamptons estates.

cards.front: Lenz Winery: in what year were its first vines planted at Peconic?

cards.front: Why does a Lenz Old Vines Merlot often reach the market years after its vintage?

records.place: Aquebogue, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: The family's estate at Aquebogue on the North Fork, a former potato farm, with the Chenin Blanc first found in a neighbouring vineyard bought in 1989 and planted further from 2000.
wine.making: Fermented slowly at cool temperatures in stainless steel tanks, with no oak, to keep its fruit and its acidity. It is bottled young under screw cap, which the house took up early among Long Island wineries, to hold its freshness.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, green apple and pineapple over pear and a touch of guava; dry, crisp and racy, light to medium in body, with a savoury, briny edge from the sea air.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in its first few years for its freshness, though a good vintage keeps and grows rounder over five years or so.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass. Oysters and white fish suit it.

label.means: The grape of the Loire's Vouvray and Savennières, rare on Long Island.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Paumanok Vineyards' Chenin Blanc is the North Fork's Chenin, from a family estate at Aquebogue: fermented cool in steel, unoaked and under screw cap, it is dry and racy with grapefruit and a briny edge. Pour it cold with oysters.
records.story: Paumanok Vineyards was founded in 1983 on a former potato farm at Aquebogue on the North Fork, when a couple planted its first vines: she came from a winegrowing family of the Pfalz in Germany, he from a background of hospitality in Lebanon. The Chenin Blanc came by accident. In 1989 the family bought a neighbouring vineyard planted to many grapes, Chenin Blanc among them, and meant to pull most of them out; they ran out of time before the Chenin went, made a little wine from it, and liked it. They kept it, planted more in 2000 and 2005 and a new clone in 2012, and Chenin Blanc became the house's white of record, by the house's own account the first made in New York. The estate was an early taker of screw caps on Long Island. In 2018 the family bought Palmer Vineyards, its neighbour at Aquebogue, also founded in 1983, and from then the founders' son made the wine of both. For a sommelier, Paumanok's Chenin is the white that shows the North Fork's acid and salt in a grape few guests expect there.

others.name: Riesling
others.note: A white of the grape of the Pfalz, where one of the founders grew up.

others.name: Cabernet Sauvignon

cards.front: How is Paumanok's Chenin Blanc fermented, and how is it closed?

The Chenin accident of 1989 rests on the New York Cork Report (Long Island Wine Press) and a New York Times account read through search; the Times gives three acres of Chenin in the vineyard bought, which the record does not teach.
The later plantings of 2000, 2005 and the new clone in 2012 rest on two local press accounts read through one search summary; the checker may want to confirm them.

The glass note follows the house's own note for the 2025 vintage (grapefruit, pineapple, pear, guava, racy) and the New York Times' savoury maritime edge.

records.place: Sagaponack, The Hamptons, Long Island, New York

wine.name: Estate Rosé
wine.grapes: Merlot, the larger part, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay and small touches of other grapes, white and red, in a blend that changes each year.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyard at Sagaponack on the South Fork, once potato fields near the Atlantic shore, on the South Fork's loam.
wine.making: Each grape is picked in its own wave, at the moment the house judges it ready, to keep the character of each. The wines are made separately and blended, and the rosé is given extended contact with its lees before it is bottled young for the summer.
wine.glass: Pale salmon pink; wild strawberry, white peach and pink grapefruit with a touch of rose petal and a saline, chalky edge; dry, light in body and crisp.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in the summer after the vintage, it keeps its freshness for a year or two.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's original rosé, the first it made, distinct from its Summer in a Bottle range.
The American Viticultural Area of the whole island, approved in 2001.

records.table: Wölffer Estate's Estate Rosé comes from Sagaponack in the Hamptons, on the South Fork: Merlot led, each grape picked in its own wave, pale, dry and crisp. It is the wine that taught the Hamptons to drink rosé, so pour it cold.
records.story: In 1978 a Hamburg born investor bought a parcel of farmland with a farmhouse among the potato fields of Sagaponack on the South Fork, and in 1988 he planted his first vineyard there, of Chardonnay, under the name Sagpond Vineyards. A German winemaker joined in 1992, and by the house's timeline the first Sagpond rosé followed in the early 1990s: the story goes that it began after a summer party where the guests were all drinking rosé from France. The winery took the founder's name, Wölffer, in 1996, by its own timeline. The pale, dry Estate Rosé grew with the Hamptons' taste for rosé until it became the summer wine of the South Fork, and the estate kept horses and stables beside its vines. The founder died in a swimming accident in Brazil on the last day of 2008, and his children carried the estate on with the winemaker. The house later added the Summer in a Bottle rosés, a separate line, and a cuvée of Merlot from its oldest field, planted in 1990, named for the founder. For a sommelier, the Estate Rosé is the American rosé that made pale and dry the fashion on the East Coast.

others.name: Christian's Cuvée Merlot
others.note: The house's red named for its founder, from its oldest Merlot field, planted in 1990.

others.name: Summer in a Bottle Rosé
others.note: A separate rosé line, picked days later than the Estate Rosé for a riper style.

Wölffer is at Sagaponack in the Hamptons on the South Fork, not on the North Fork where most Long Island estates lie.

The making follows the house's 2025 technical note (picked in waves, extended lees contact); no press method or vessel was found and none is taught; the Long Island appellation on the label rests on the house's product pages.

records.place: Mattituck, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Bergen Road
wine.grapes: A blend of the Bordeaux grapes led by Merlot, with Cabernet Sauvignon and, by the year, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot or Malbec.
wine.sites: The family's waterfront farm at Mattituck on the bluffs above Long Island Sound, on sandy glacial soils, farmed with biodynamic principles from its first plantings.
wine.making: Made only in the vintages the family judges strong enough, from the estate's own grapes, with the blend of the Bordeaux grapes settled anew each year. It is aged in oak barrels for well over a year before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and blackcurrant with cedar, tobacco and a note of graphite; medium to full in body, with fresh acidity and firm, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it opens after five years or so and a strong vintage keeps well into its second decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's flagship red blend, made only in strong vintages.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Bergen Road is Macari Vineyards' flagship red from Mattituck on the North Fork, made only in strong years: a Merlot led blend of the Bordeaux grapes from a biodynamically farmed estate above the Sound. It is firm and fresh, so decant it.
records.story: The Macari family owned a waterfront farm at Mattituck, on the bluffs above Long Island Sound, for decades before it held a vine; by the house's account the land had been in the family since the 1960s. In 1995, twenty two years after the first vinifera of Long Island went in at Cutchogue in 1973, father, son and daughter in law planted the first vineyard there and founded Macari Vineyards. From the first plantings the family farmed by biodynamic principles, making its own compost and keeping a herd of longhorn cattle on the farm for their manure and for the horn preparations biodynamic farming uses. Bergen Road became the house's flagship red, a blend of the Bordeaux grapes made only in the vintages the family judges strong enough and settled anew each time. The house later opened a second tasting room at Cutchogue. For a sommelier, Bergen Road is the red that shows biodynamic farming on Long Island, and a study in how the North Fork's Merlot and Cabernet are blended.

others.note: The house's reserve red, made beside Bergen Road.

others.note: A crisp white from the estate above the Sound.
